## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Session 2: Kaplan-Meier curves by group
- Today: **are the curves different** beyond chance?
- By the end you can:
  - run and read a **log-rank test**
  - use **observed vs expected** deaths to give the direction
  - **stratify** a log-rank test
  - explain why a **t-test of follow-up time** is wrong
:::

# Topic 1 — The log-rank test {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## What it compares

At every event time, given how many are at risk in each group, how many deaths would we **expect** in each group **if the curves were the same**? The test adds up (observed − expected) over all event times.

::: {.key}
**H₀:** the survival curves (hazards) are the **same** in all groups. Small p: evidence of a **difference somewhere along follow-up**. It uses the **whole curve**, and is most powerful when the hazards are **proportional**.
:::

## HIV status

```{r}
lr_hiv <- survdiff(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hiv, data = tb)
lr_hiv
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Observed** vs **expected** deaths: HIV-positive patients had more deaths than expected (`r lr_hiv$obs[2]` vs `r round(lr_hiv$exp[2], 1)`)
- `Chisq` on **1 df** and its p-value: here p = `r signif(1 - pchisq(lr_hiv$chisq, 1), 2)`
- The test gives **no size of effect**: use the hazard ratio (Session 4)
:::

## A null result

```{r}
lr_sex <- survdiff(Surv(time_months, status) ~ sex, data = tb)
c(chisq = round(lr_sex$chisq, 2), p = round(1 - pchisq(lr_sex$chisq, 1), 2))
```

::: {.warn}
p = `r round(1 - pchisq(lr_sex$chisq, 1), 2)` means **no evidence** of a difference by sex, **not proof** of none: look at the **CI of the hazard ratio** to see which differences remain plausible.
:::

# Topic 2 — Getting it right {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Stratified log-rank

Compare HIV groups **within** treatment arms, then combine:

```{r}
survdiff(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hiv + strata(treatment), data = tb)
```

::: {.incremental}
- Use when another variable also affects survival and is **unbalanced** between the groups
- It cannot compare the stratifying variable itself, and **adjusts for one factor at a time**: for several, use Cox
:::

## More than two groups

```{r}
tb |> mutate(group = case_when(mdr_tb == "Yes" ~ "MDR-TB", hiv == "Positive" ~ "HIV, drug-sensitive", TRUE ~ "Drug-sensitive, HIV-negative")) |>
  survdiff(Surv(time_months, status) ~ group, data = _)
```

An **overall** test on k groups has **k − 1 df**; it says *some* group differs. Follow with pairwise comparisons, **adjusted** for multiple testing.

## The wrong tests

::: {.bad}
- **t-test or Wilcoxon on follow-up time:** mixes deaths and censored times, and answers a different question
- **Chi-square on "died yes/no"** ignores follow-up time, which differs between patients
:::

```{r}
c(t_test = signif(t.test(time_months ~ hiv, data = tb)$p.value, 2), log_rank = signif(1 - pchisq(lr_hiv$chisq, 1), 2))
```

## The log-rank test does not

::: {.incremental}
- **Adjust** for several covariates: use **Cox regression**
- Give an **effect size**: report the **hazard ratio with a CI**
- Work well when the **curves cross**: then the "average" difference can be near zero while the curves differ early and late
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s3q1", "What is the null hypothesis of the log-rank test comparing two groups?",
         c("The median survival time is the same in both groups",
           "The numbers of patients at the start are equal in both groups",
           "The survival curves are the same in both groups",
           "The hazard ratio is exactly 1 at one particular time"), answer = 3,
         explain = "The log-rank test asks whether the two survival (hazard) curves coincide over the whole follow-up. It does not compare only a median or one time point.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s3q2", "HIV-positive patients had 19 observed deaths and 11.4 expected. How should this be read?",
         c("Fewer deaths than expected if survival were the same in both groups",
           "More deaths than expected if survival were the same in both groups",
           "The test has failed, because the two numbers are different",
           "A difference of 7.6 deaths per 100 person-years"), answer = 2,
         explain = "Expected deaths are what the group would have if the curves were identical. A group with more deaths than expected fared worse than the pooled experience.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s3q3", "Why is a t-test on the follow-up time of two groups inappropriate for survival data?",
         c("The t-test needs both of the groups to have the same number of patients",
           "Follow-up times follow a normal distribution in a typical sample of patients",
           "Follow-up times mix deaths and censored times, so it asks the wrong question",
           "A t-test can be used for yes/no outcomes and not for times to an event"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Censored times are not death times, so comparing average follow-up times does not compare survival. The log-rank test uses the censoring information correctly.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s3q4", "The log-rank test by sex gives p = 0.63. Which conclusion is best?",
         c("Men and women have been shown to have identical survival in the cohort",
           "Sex has no effect on survival in any population of TB patients",
           "The test was underpowered, so it should be repeated on more patients",
           "No evidence of a difference in survival by sex in this cohort"), answer = 4,
         explain = "A large p-value is weak evidence against 'no difference', not proof of equality. The hazard ratio and its CI show which differences are still plausible.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s3q5", "When is a stratified log-rank test most useful?",
         c("When another factor affects survival and is unbalanced between groups",
           "When the survival curves of the two groups cross over each other once",
           "When there are no deaths recorded in one of the two groups compared",
           "When the follow-up times of the patients are normally distributed"), answer = 1,
         explain = "Stratification compares groups within levels of another variable and combines the results, so imbalance in that variable does not distort the comparison.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- **Log-rank**: compares the whole curves; H₀ = same survival
- **Observed vs expected** deaths give the direction
- Stratify for **one** other factor; use **Cox** for several
- Never t-test follow-up times; a non-significant p is not proof of no difference
:::
